caveats: **Coverage is a fixed set of stores, not everything the device trusts.** Windows reads the machine stores `MY`, `ROOT`, `CA` and `Trust`; Linux reads `.pem` and `.crt` files directly in `/etc/ssl/certs` and only the first certificate in each; macOS reads the System, system-root and (with a console user, and as root) login keychains. Trust settings, the Windows disallowed store, application-private bundles and any other trust-store location are not read, so presence in a listed store does not prove a certificate is trusted for every purpose.

**Linux `delete` is coarse and keeps a narrow race.** It removes the first matching directory entry as a whole, so a file holding several certificates goes with its first one, and a symlink is removed without touching its target. POSIX has no unlink by descriptor, so a small window remains between the identity re-check and `unlinkat`, and because identity is inode and link text rather than content, an in-place rewrite of the same file in that window is not detected.

**macOS `delete` covers the System keychain only, and the login keychain read is a subprocess.** `SystemRootCertificates.keychain` is sealed by System Integrity Protection and is rejected, and `login` and `all` are rejected for `delete` rather than redirected. The login-keychain read runs through `launchctl asuser` and `sudo -u`, works only because the daemon runs as root today, and the console-owner re-check narrows but does not close the fast-user-switch race.

**Degraded reads are disclosed, with one quiet exception.** An unopenable or incomplete store, an unreadable file, a timed-out keychain or an unavailable login keychain each produces a `not_available` row and a `CONSTRAINED` / `PARTIAL` status. A Linux host with no `/etc/ssl/certs` directory returns the header row alone with no status, which looks the same as an empty store.

**The macOS sample was captured unprivileged, and test-only overrides exist.** The sample shows the login-keychain read degrading and never a successful one. The `YUZU_CERTIFICATES_SYSTEM_KEYCHAIN_PATH_OVERRIDE`, `YUZU_CERTIFICATES_ROOT_KEYCHAIN_PATH_OVERRIDE`, `YUZU_CERTIFICATES_CONSOLE_USER_OVERRIDE`, `YUZU_CERTIFICATES_CONSOLE_OWNER_UID_OVERRIDE` and `YUZU_CERTIFICATES_LOGIN_KEYCHAIN_READ_FAIL_OVERRIDE` environment variables redirect or simulate those reads for unit tests and must never be set in production; `delete` ignores the keychain path overrides.

definitions.description: Delete a certificate from a system store by SHA-1 thumbprint. On Windows this targets a specific named store (defaults to MY). On Linux it removes the matching PEM/CRT file from /etc/ssl/certs/. On macOS it uses the security CLI to delete from System.keychain by default; store=root is rejected as unsupported (returns a non-zero exit code) because SystemRootCertificates.keychain is sealed by System Integrity Protection on modern macOS and cannot actually be modified. A macOS delete verifies the certificate is actually absent from the target keychain afterward before reporting success. This is a destructive action and requires approval.
Retrieve full details for a specific certificate identified by its SHA-1 thumbprint. Searches all available certificate stores on the device.

Enumerate certificates in system certificate stores. On Windows this queries the CryptoAPI stores (MY, ROOT, CA, Trust). On Linux it parses PEM files in /etc/ssl/certs/. On macOS it reads System.keychain and SystemRootCertificates.keychain, plus the current console user's login keychain when one is logged in. Results can be filtered by store name and by expiration window.

description: Certificate inventory and management for system stores
how_it_works:
`list` and `details` read the certificates held in the operating system's own trust stores and emit one eight-field row per certificate; `list` returns every match (filtered by `store` and `expiring_within_days`) and `details` returns the row whose SHA-1 thumbprint matches, or `status|not_found`. `delete` removes one certificate by thumbprint from one store. It validates the thumbprint as 40 hex characters first, acts on exactly one named store, and reports `status|deleted`, `status|not_found`, `status|delete_failed` (Windows and Linux, when the removal itself fails) or an `error|...` line with a non-zero exit. The plugin does not build or validate a trust chain, check revocation, import or renew certificates, or read stores other than those named below.

Windows reads the CryptoAPI stores `MY`, `ROOT`, `CA` and `Trust` in process under the LocalMachine hive; a read falls back to CurrentUser if LocalMachine cannot be opened and says so, but `delete` never falls back. Linux reads the `.pem` and `.crt` files directly under `/etc/ssl/certs` and parses them in process with libcrypto; only the first certificate in each file is read. macOS reads `System.keychain` and `SystemRootCertificates.keychain` in process through the Security framework (15 seconds per keychain) and the console user's login keychain through a subprocess: `launchctl asuser` and `sudo -u` run `security find-certificate`, and each returned block is parsed by `/usr/bin/openssl`. Before that spawn the agent re-checks the owner of `/dev/console` and refuses to read if it changed. Every macOS action runs inside a shared 60-second budget, so a wedged directory service shows as a `not_available` row with `CONSTRAINED` status rather than a hang.

`delete` is destructive and cannot be undone by Yuzu; the certificate has to be re-imported by other means. On macOS it first proves the certificate is present (an absent one is `status|not_found`, not a command failure), runs `security delete-certificate` against `System.keychain`, then re-reads the keychain and reports `deleted` only if the certificate is gone. On Linux it removes the matching directory entry (a symlink is removed, never its target) after re-checking the entry's identity immediately before `unlinkat`. The plugin does not run `update-ca-certificates` or edit any combined bundle.

The diagram shows where each OS leg gets its data. Reads need Security read; `delete` needs Security delete, is classed Destructive and is gated on an administrator or an approval.

### What you can decide with it

| Question | Action | Windows | macOS | Linux |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Which certificates does this device trust? | `list` | Machine stores `ROOT`, `CA`, `Trust` and `MY`. Per-user stores are read only as a disclosed fallback. | System and system-root keychains, plus the login keychain when a user is at the console. | Files named `*.pem` or `*.crt` in `/etc/ssl/certs`, first certificate of each file. |
| What expires soon? | `list` with `expiring_within_days` | Same filter on `not_after`. | Same. | Same. |
| Is this specific certificate present, and where? | `details` with a thumbprint | Searches all four stores. | `store` narrows to `login`, `System`, `root` or `all`. | Searches the directory. |
| Which certificates are not from the usual public authorities? | `list`, compare `issuer` and `subject` against a known list | Yes. | Yes. | Yes. |
| Remove a rogue or expired certificate | `delete` | Named store, LocalMachine only. | `System.keychain` only. | The matching file or link in `/etc/ssl/certs`. |

`expiring_within_days=N` keeps certificates whose `not_after` is within N days, including ones that have already expired, and any whose date could not be parsed. `0` returns everything.

Safe workflow for `delete`: run `details` with the thumbprint to confirm the exact store and subject, dispatch `delete` to that one device with the same thumbprint and store, then run `details` again; it should report `status|not_found`. There is no preview and no undo. On macOS the root keychain is sealed by System Integrity Protection, so `delete` with `store=root`, `login` or `all` is rejected rather than redirected. On Linux, a file holding several certificates is removed whole when its first certificate matches.

What a result does and does not prove:

- Presence in a store is not the same as being trusted for every purpose. The plugin reads store contents only; it does not read macOS trust settings, Windows disallowed lists or application-specific bundles.
- A `CONSTRAINED` status or a `not_available` row means part of the inventory is missing. Treat the list as incomplete, never as "nothing there".
- An empty Linux list with no status means `/etc/ssl/certs` does not exist. Distributions that keep trust anchors elsewhere are not covered.
- Thumbprints identify certificates, not devices or people, but `subject` for code-signing certificates is effectively a software-publisher list (see Sensitivity).

### Diagrams

Linux `delete` binds to one directory handle for the whole operation, so a swapped directory cannot redirect it:

If the entry's identity changed since the match, or cannot be re-derived, nothing is removed and the result is `CONSTRAINED` with `posix:delete-recheck`. If any entry could not be read, the scan cannot prove the certificate is absent, so it reports an error rather than `not_found`. Identity is inode and link text, not content, so an in-place rewrite of the same file between match and unlink is not detected.

macOS `delete` proves its own result:

The first absent answer short-circuits to `not_found` only when the read was definitive. Exit code zero from `security` is never trusted on its own: if the keychain cannot be re-read, or still holds the certificate, the result is an `error` and the exit code is non-zero.

Windows store fallback differs between reads and `delete`:

A CurrentUser fallback row is announced by a `not_available` line before that store's rows and marks the result `CONSTRAINED` with `cryptoapi:store-fallback`. `delete` has no CurrentUser path: an unopenable store is `error|<store> store could not be opened; nothing removed`.

inputs.description: SHA-1 thumbprint (hex string, no colons) of the certificate to delete. Case-insensitive.
inputs.name: thumbprint

inputs.description: The certificate store to delete from. On Windows: MY, ROOT, CA, or Trust. Defaults to "MY". On macOS: "MY" (the default) or "System" deletes from /Library/Keychains/System.keychain, matching prior behaviour. "root" is REJECTED (non-zero exit, unsupported) -- SystemRootCertificates.keychain is sealed by System Integrity Protection on modern macOS and cannot actually be modified, so attempting it would report a change that never took effect. "login" and "all" are also not supported for delete and are rejected with an error rather than silently deleting from an unintended store, as is any other unrecognized value. Ignored on Linux. On Windows the named store is opened under the LocalMachine hive only; if it cannot be opened there the action reports error|<store> store could not be opened; nothing removed (non-zero exit) and never falls back to the CurrentUser hive.

columns.description: A successful macOS delete emits status|deleted; a delete targeting a certificate already provably absent from the keychain emits status|not_found (rc 0), matching the Windows/Linux contract for an absent cert. store=root is rejected with error|MESSAGE (SystemRootCertificates.keychain is sealed by System Integrity Protection). Every other macOS rejection or failure -- an unsupported store, a failed delete command, or a post-delete verification that still finds the certificate or could not re-read the keychain -- also emits error|MESSAGE. outputs_note: `list` and `details` write a header row followed by zero or more pipe-delimited certificate rows, or a `status|not_found` / `not_available|<reason>` line in place of a row when nothing matched or a store couldn't be read; on Windows, a `not_available|<store> store (LocalMachine) could not be opened; rows read from CurrentUser` line precedes that store's own rows rather than replacing them, disclosing the CurrentUser fallback. `delete` writes one line only: `status|<value>`, `error|<message>`, or (macOS only) `not_available|<reason>`. `(unknown)` is the honest per-field sentinel for a value that failed to parse — it never means zero or empty; `subject`/`issuer`/`serial`/`key_usage` are escaped so a hostile value can never inject an extra pipe-delimited column or newline-delimited row.

privileges.grant: `list` and `details`: none, since reading the machine stores needs no elevation. `delete`: the plugin requests and enables no privilege of its own; the write to a LocalMachine store succeeds as `SYSTEM`. `docs/agent-privilege-model.md` lists `SeBackupPrivilege` and `SeRestorePrivilege` for this action, but nothing in the plugin code uses or requires either, and a narrower account has not been measured
privileges.if_refused: A store that cannot be opened (even after the CurrentUser fallback) is a `not_available` row with `CONSTRAINED` and `cryptoapi:store-open`; one that ends abnormally is `cryptoapi:store-enum`. `details` never reports `not_found` for a store it could not fully read; it reports one combined scan-incomplete row. `delete` opens LocalMachine only and reports `error` with a non-zero exit, never `not_found`
privileges.measured: `SYSTEM` on bare-metal Windows 10.0.26200, 2026-09-07, `list` and `details`; the captured `delete` exercises only its parameter check

privileges.grant: System and root keychains: none, read in process. Login keychain: root, through `launchctl asuser` and `sudo -n -u`; this works only because the daemon runs as root today, and a non-root agent would need the sudoers grant described in `docs/agent-privilege-model.md`. `delete` (System keychain only) runs `/usr/bin/security delete-certificate` as the daemon
privileges.if_refused: A keychain that is unreadable, times out, hits the bounded-call ceiling or is capped emits a `not_available` row naming it, with `CONSTRAINED` and provenance `secitem:<keychain>`; an empty answer counts as "zero certificates" only if the keychain's read-permission bit is set. A login-keychain failure (no console user, user changed, spawn failed) is `not_available` with `login-keychain`
privileges.measured: bare-metal macOS 26.6.2, euid 501, 2026-09-07, through the test harness rather than the root LaunchDaemon, so the sample shows the login-keychain read degrading
privileges.runs_as: agent daemon, root (the LaunchDaemon has no `UserName` key; the sample was captured unprivileged, see Measured)

privileges.grant: `list` and `details`: none, a filesystem read and in-process parse. `delete`: write permission on the `/etc/ssl/certs` directory itself, which is normally root-owned; without it the `unlinkat` fails and the result is `status|delete_failed` with a non-zero exit
privileges.if_refused: An unreadable or unparseable file is a row marked `(unreadable)` with `CONSTRAINED` and `libcrypto:unreadable-file`. A directory that cannot be opened (including a symlink or non-directory at that path) is `not_available` with `posix:cert-dir`; a listing that fails part-way is `posix:cert-enum`. An identity change between match and unlink is `error` with `posix:delete-recheck`, and nothing is removed
privileges.measured: Debian GNU/Linux 13 container, euid 0, 2026-09-06; delete as the unprivileged account is not measured
privileges.runs_as: agent daemon, dedicated unprivileged account, never root by design (`docs/agent-privilege-model.md`)

where_the_data_goes: **Instruction result.** Rows travel over the agent's mTLS gRPC channel as the command response and land in the ResponseStore (90-day default retention), queryable at `/api/responses/{id}`; `list` also aggregates by `store` and `issuer` through its definition's `aggregation` block.

**Not consumed by** daily-sync inventory, the Echo warehouse, DEX, or metrics — no reference to the `certificates` plugin or its definition ids exists outside `server/core/src/capability_decls/plugin_action_catalogue_c.hpp`.

**Sensitivity.** `list`/`details` rows carry every certificate's `subject` and `issuer` — for code-signing certs (the Windows sample) this is effectively an installed-software-publisher inventory (e.g. `Logitech Inc`, `Microsoft Corporation`) by another route, and on macOS a successful login-keychain read can surface the signed-in user's own personal certificates; `thumbprint`/`serial` uniquely identify a specific certificate but not a device or person directly.
**Siblings:** none in this plugin group; the `diagnostics.certificates` action (a different plugin, TLS cert/key diagnostics) is unrelated despite the similar name.

**MCP / REST.** Discover: `discover_plugins` (summary) → `yuzu://plugin-docs` (this page as data) → `discover_instructions` / `get_definition("security.certificates.list")`. Run: `execute_instruction {definition_id, parameters}`. Read: `/api/responses/{id}`.
